mendico , āvi, ātum, 1, v. n. and
I.a., and mendīcor , ātus sum (archaio inf. mendicarier, Plaut. Capt. prol. 13), 1, v. dep. id., to beg, ask for alms, go a-begging; to beg for something, solicit, obtain by begging; constr. absol. and with acc. (poet. and post-class.): mendicantem vivere, to
live by begging. Plaut. Capt 2, 2, 73: “quando histrionem cogis mendicarier,” id. ib. prol. 13; “mendicum malim mendicando vincere,” id. ib. 3, 4, 16 .—Act.: “a me mendicas malum,” Plaut. Am. 4, 2, 12 : “aliquid mendicare,” App. Mag. p. 287, 1 .—Poet.: “ejectis mendicat silva Camenis,” i.e. is full of beggars, Juv. 3, 16 .—Part. in pass. sense: “mendicatus victa Karthagine panis,” Juv. 10, 277 .
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
